exam: What immediate assessment differentiates acute psychosis from delirium? — Check level of consciousness, attention, and fluctuation; delirium shows impaired attention and fluctuating alertness.

A patient with new‑onset psychosis tests HIV‑positive. How does this change management? — Initiate ART, screen for opportunistic infections, and consider HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder as a cause.
Why is high‑dose chlorpromazine avoided in a patient with known cardiac disease? — It prolongs QT interval and can precipitate torsades de pointes.

In a resource‑limited ward, CSF analysis is unavailable but TB meningitis is suspected. What is the best next step? — Start empirical anti‑TB therapy with steroids while arranging transfer if possible.
How would you explain the need for a benzodiazepine trial before antipsychotics in catatonia? — Catatonia may worsen with antipsychotics; lorazepam can rapidly improve symptoms and confirm diagnosis.
What psychosocial intervention is most feasible in an East African community setting? — Involve family and community health workers for medication supervision and psycho‑education.

A patient on haloperidol develops rigidity and fever. What complication should you suspect and how to manage? — Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop antipsychotic, give supportive care, consider dantrolene if available.
How does the BPRS score guide severity staging? — Scores ≤31 indicate mild, 32‑45 moderate, >45 severe psychosis, guiding treatment intensity.
ai.title: Understanding Psychosis
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Psychosis is a state of impaired reality testing with delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, abnormal behavior, and negative symptoms. Recognise severity, common tropical causes, and manage with antipsychotics and psychosocial support in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Psychosis is a syndrome of disturbed perception or thought, defined by at least two of five DSM‑5‑TR features lasting >1 day, with functional impairment.
Use the Clinical Global Impression‑Severity (CGI‑S) and the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) to stage mild, moderate, severe, and chronic psychosis.
Identify reversible and primary causes; in East Africa infections and substance use are common precipitants.
Patients may be agitated, withdrawn, or confused; look for delusional content, auditory hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and functional decline.
Prioritise tests that clarify reversible causes; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Detect anemia, infection, or leukocytosis; anemia may suggest malaria or HIV‑related marrow suppression
Identify HIV infection; a positive result prompts ART and opportunistic infection screening
Rule out metabolic derangements (e.g., hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia) that can mimic psychosis
Look for lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein; if unavailable, treat empirically for TB meningitis when clinical suspicion high
Identify stimulant or hallucinogen use; if unavailable, rely on history and clinical clues
